title: Fluid Template Files and Their Namespaces

hints.text: Template files carry the .fluid.html extension. The bare .html form still resolves, so a directory of .html templates is the predecessor rather than a mistake to fix on sight.
Template files carry the bare .html extension. The .fluid.html form is not resolved here.

hints: Which of two files that both exist is the one rendered is decided per root path: TemplatePaths::resolveFileInPaths() walks the root paths backwards and tries the whole chain of candidate file names inside each one before moving to the next. So the later root path overloads the earlier one whatever file name extension either side carries, and the file name never decides between two root paths.

Later is the array and not the call. TYPO3\CMS\Fluid\View\TemplatePaths sorts every root path list by its integer key on the way in, through ArrayUtility::sortArrayWithIntegerKeys(), so the highest key wins: a path appended without a key of its own — from an event listener, say — takes max+1 and does win, while one given an explicitly lower key loses however late it was set. The sort is skipped for the whole list as soon as one key in it is a string, and then the array's own order decides after all.

A template, unlike a layout or a partial, is looked for under the controller directory across every root path first, and only then directly under the root paths. A root path holding List/Default.html therefore answers before a later one holding Default.html.

hints.text: Inside one root path the candidates are Foo.fluid.html, Foo.html, a bare Foo, and then those three again with the first character uppercased. So .fluid.html wins over .html in the same directory; the spelling that was asked for is tried before the uppercased one, which is why a template file no longer has to begin with a capital; and an extension's own Login.html still overloads the core's Login.fluid.html when its root path is the later one.

The new extension may not be used by an extension that still supports an older TYPO3 major, where Fluid does not look for *.fluid.* at all. Such an extension ships .html, which a sitepackage on this major overloads with either name.

A name that carries its own file extension leaves the chain. <f:render partial="Foo.html" /> from a template in format json is looked for as Foo.html.fluid.json, Foo.html.json and then bare Foo.html, so it finds a Foo.html file and never a Foo.fluid.html one — that reference is written out in full.

Inside one root path the candidates are Foo.html and then a bare Foo. There is no .fluid.html candidate and no uppercase fallback in the file names here: the action name is capitalised before the lookup, so the file is spelled the way the caller spells it.

hints: Only a few prefixes are available without declaring them, and which ones depends on what is installed. typo3_fluid_namespace_list answers it for your installation.

hints.text: A package registers a global prefix through its Configuration/Fluid/Namespaces.php, which returns prefix => list of PHP namespaces and is merged across every active package.
A package registers a global prefix by adding to $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SYS']['fluid']['namespaces'] in its ext_localconf.php. There is no Configuration/Fluid/Namespaces.php on this major.

hints: Every other namespace is declared per template, including the backend one: xmlns:be="http://typo3.org/ns/TYPO3/CMS/Backend/ViewHelpers" on the root element, together with data-namespace-typo3-fluid="true" so the declaration is stripped from the rendered output.
Use typo3_component_lookup for the markup of a backend component and typo3_icon_lookup for an icon identifier, instead of writing either from memory.

A core ViewHelper's argument list is in the manual rather than in this corpus. typo3_documentation_lookup answers a query like f:for each ViewHelper with that ViewHelper's page in the Fluid ViewHelper Reference, and passing that page back reads out its Arguments section: every argument with its type, its default, and whether it is required.

A ViewHelper outside the core is in no reference and is read from the class its identifier names. The prefix stands for a PHP namespace — typo3_fluid_namespace_list for a globally registered one, the xmlns declaration for one declared in the template — and the rest of the identifier is the class below it, every dot-separated segment uppercased and ViewHelper appended: my:foo.bar is My\Package\ViewHelpers\Foo\BarViewHelper. Where a prefix carries several namespaces the last one registered is tried first. That class's registerArgument() calls are the argument list.
What a template may and may not do is fluid-layouts-sections, where an expression goes wrong is fluid-conditions-and-arrays, and what {obj.foo} asks the object is fluid-object-access.

title: How a Backend Module Resolves a Fluid Template

hints.text: A backend module resolves templates through the templateRootPaths of its view factory, so a partial is referenced by its name below Resources/Private/Partials, never by a file path.

There is no view factory here: a backend module builds its own view — StandaloneView with setTemplateRootPaths() and setPartialRootPaths(), or the Extbase view of an Extbase module — and the rule is the same, a partial is referenced by its name rather than by a file path.

title: What a Fluid Layout Renders, and What Is Never Executed
hints: A template that declares a layout renders its sections and nothing else. Markup, an <f:variable> assignment or any other ViewHelper call outside <f:section> is never executed — the layout is rendered in place of the template body, so the value is simply absent, no error is raised and nothing is logged. A variable a section uses is declared inside that section.

<f:asset.css> and <f:asset.script> are where that is invisible: they render nothing where they stand and register the file with the AssetCollector instead. A call outside a section leaves the stylesheet published under _assets and no link tag in the rendered page. Nothing requests the file, so there is no HTTP 404 to find either. The call belongs inside the section that needs the asset, or in the layout.

Notes in a template belong in <f:comment>, whose children are not rendered at all. An HTML comment is part of the response, and the {expressions} inside it are resolved on the way there — a comment that documents the variables of a loop ships their values to the browser.

title: Fluid Conditions, Escaping and Array Literals
hints: Fluid escapes output by default. Do not work around it in the template; if a ViewHelper has to return markup, that decision belongs in the ViewHelper via escapeOutput.

A comparison inside a condition attribute is written with single quotes: condition="{cell} != ''". With double quotes, condition="{cell}!="", the attribute value ends at the second double quote, what follows matches no ViewHelper tag, and the template stops at the closing tag with "You closed a templating tag which you never opened!", exception 1224485838. It is reported at the line of the </f:if> rather than at the condition's, so the line number in the message points away from the defect. The same holds for any attribute value carrying a string literal.

A bare condition="{value}" is false for every spelling of zero, not only for empty and null: BooleanNode::convertToBoolean() sends anything is_numeric() accepts through (bool)(float), so 0, "0", a string of two zeros and a zero written with a decimal point all take the else branch. PHP's own casting does not — it reads the last two as true — so a value an editor legitimately typed disappears into whatever the else branch is, usually a placeholder. condition="{cell} != ''" is what tells an empty value from a zero.

Once an <f:if> carries an <f:else>, its then-branch has to be an explicit <f:then>. Without one the markup between <f:if> and <f:else> is no branch at all: with the condition true it renders nothing, a ViewHelper standing there is never called, no error is raised and nothing is logged — the else content is what appears. An <f:else if="..."> child does the same. Only an <f:if> that has neither renders its inline body as the then-branch. The working shape is <f:if condition="{testimonial.data.link}"><f:then><f:link.typolink parameter="{testimonial.data.link}">{testimonial.data.company}</f:link.typolink></f:then><f:else>{testimonial.data.company}</f:else></f:if>.

An array literal needs at least one key-value pair: there is no {} and it is not an empty array. It evaluates to null wherever it stands — an attribute value, an inline argument, the body of an f:variable — and a null argument is not one that was given, so the ViewHelper gets the default declared for it. additionalParams="{}" therefore passes no array rather than an empty one, which is usually what was meant anyway.

hints.text: An array-typed argument that has to be absent under a condition is therefore one call and not two: additionalParams="{f:if(condition: c, then: params)}" evaluates to null when the condition is false, which is the same as leaving the argument out. The array in then may be a variable or a literal; both arrive as an array.

An array-typed argument that has to be absent under a condition needs two calls here, one in f:then and one in f:else. Written as one — additionalParams="{f:if(condition: c, then: params)}" — it hands the argument an empty string instead, because an f:if with no else evaluates to that rather than to null. A ViewHelper that casts it then builds a query parameter out of nothing, (array)'' being a one-element array holding an empty string, and nothing reports it.

title: How Fluid Resolves an Object Path, and the Method That Shadows a Property
appliesTo: naming a method on a DTO
hints: A path segment is resolved by StandardVariableProvider::getByPath(), which takes the first thing of that name it finds: an array key or an ArrayAccess offset, then getFoo(), then isFoo(), then hasFoo(), and the public property foo last. A segment that matches none of them makes the whole path null, which renders as nothing.

hints.text: A PSR-11 container is asked ahead of all of them, has() and then get() for the segment. preview-record-variable is that branch for the one variable a backend preview template is handed.

hints: So a method is reachable under the name of the property it looks like, never under its own. {obj.hasItems} makes Fluid look for getHasItems(), isHasItems(), hasHasItems() and a hasItems property, and never for the hasItems() somebody wrote. The core writes the convention the other way round: SlidingWindowPagination declares getHasMorePages(), and the redirects pagination partial reads it as {pagination.hasMorePages}.

The same order lets a boolean shadow the array it is about. A hasItems() beside a public array $items makes {obj.items} the boolean, rendered as 1 or as nothing, and the array cannot be reached from the template at all. A DTO that templates read therefore gets no has<Property>() or is<Property>() for a property of that name: write a count as get<Property>Count(), and keep a boolean name for something no property is called.

hints.text: <f:for each="{obj.items}"> then stops the render, for a true and for a false alike: "The argument "each" was registered with type "array", but is of type "boolean"". What that names is the ViewHelper and never the method the value came from.

<f:for each="{obj.items}"> then stops the render where the boolean is true: "The argument "each" was registered with type "array", but is of type "boolean"". What that names is the ViewHelper and never the method the value came from.

Where the boolean is false, nothing is raised at all. The lenient check passes every empty value, so the loop is skipped over it, and what is left in its place is a PHP warning — foreach() argument must be of type array|object — which the shipped exceptionalErrors does not turn into an exception.

And the message survives only as long as the template is uncompiled. ForViewHelper is compiled into a direct renderStatic() call, which skips validateArguments() altogether, so the exception appears on the first render and a warm fluid_template cache renders the loop as nothing from then on.

title: ViewHelpers
hints: The current shape is a final class extending AbstractViewHelper with initializeArguments(): void declaring every argument through registerArgument(), and a typed render(): string. Dependencies are constructor-injected.

hints.text: renderStatic() and the CompileWithRenderStatic trait are the predecessor of that shape and are on their way out: no core ViewHelper carries them any more. Do not write a new one with them; whether your branch already marks them deprecated is in its own changelog and extension scanner matchers.
The core still writes ViewHelpers with renderStatic() and the CompileWithRenderStatic trait here, and both shapes work. A new one is better written with render().

hints: Set protected bool $escapeOutput = false when the ViewHelper returns markup, and $escapeChildren = false when its children are markup rather than text. Both are opt-outs from Fluid's default escaping, so state why in the class docblock.

hints.text: The type in registerArgument() is enforced on every argument that was given, and a value that does not match it stops the render: "The argument "x" was registered with type "array", but is of type "string"". An empty string is what usually walks into that — a variable assigned "", or a template expression that came back empty — because null does not: a null argument counts as not given and the declared default is used instead. Which strictness applies is an injectable service, ArgumentProcessorInterface, and the strict one is what an installation gets unless it says otherwise.

A value that does not match the type declared in registerArgument() stops the render here too — "The argument "x" was registered with type "array", but is of type "string"" — and the lenient check this branch runs has one hole in it: every empty value passes whatever the type says. An empty string therefore reaches an array-typed argument as a string, and what happens next is that ViewHelper's own cast rather than an error — so the render succeeds and the output is wrong.

hints: Only an argument no registerArgument() call declares reaches $this->additionalArguments on a tag-based ViewHelper, and initialize() pushes those onto the TagBuilder before render() runs. So registering such an attribute takes it out of $this->tag->getAttributes() too, and a ViewHelper that reads its own attributes back stops finding the value, with nothing raised.

TagBuilder emits its attributes in the order they were added, and initialize() adds the unregistered ones before render() runs. So an attribute that becomes a registered argument also moves in the rendered tag, to wherever the render puts it back.

hints.text: registerTagAttribute() declares an argument and has initialize() put it on the tag, so registering an attribute this way does not take it off the rendered tag. It and registerUniversalTagAttributes() are deprecated.

hints: ViewHelpers are covered by functional tests under Tests/Functional/ViewHelpers/, not unit tests: a ViewHelper needs a rendering context, so a unit test asserts the wrong thing.

hints.text: A ViewHelper is public API. A new one, or a changed argument list, needs a changelog entry under typo3/sysext/core/Documentation/Changelog/, in the directory of the minor version it is released in. Which of the four types the entry is, and what it has to contain, is documentation-changelog.

hints: Fluid parsing itself is configured in $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SYS']['fluid'] in typo3/sysext/core/Configuration/DefaultConfiguration.php — interceptors, preProcessors including NamespaceDetectionTemplateProcessor, and expressionNodeTypes.

hints.text: The resource half of this area was rebuilt underneath that shape: a URL to an asset comes from the System Resource API rather than from the ViewHelper doing its own path arithmetic, and fluid-resource-uris is what changed.

title: Resource URIs in a Fluid Template, and Where Cache Busting Is Applied

hints.text: f:resource resolves a resource identifier into a resource object and f:uri.resource turns that object into a URI: {f:resource(identifier: 'PKG:my-vendor/site-package:Resources/Public/Css/main.css') -> f:uri.resource()}. Those two are the whole Fluid surface of the System Resource API in TYPO3\CMS\Core\SystemResource. f:image and f:uri.image are not on it — they resolve through FAL and the Extbase ImageService, and what their own class documentation says about an extension resource is the next statement. f:uri.resource also still takes a plain path with an optional extensionName, so the object form is the addition rather than the replacement.

hints: An extension resource in f:image is discouraged, not forbidden, and the two image ViewHelpers do not say the same thing about it. f:uri.image's class documentation reads "This ViewHelper should only be used for images within FAL storages, or where graphical operations shall be performed" and sends an extension resource to f:uri.resource instead. f:image says neither, and its own first example is an EXT: path into a package's Resources/Public rendered with width="100c"; the core covers that form, in SvgImageViewHelperTest, with width, height, crop and fileExtension. What both docblocks do warn about is stability rather than support: image operations on non-FAL files "may be changed in future TYPO3 versions", because each one creates a "fake" FAL record. The route behind it is ResourceFactory::retrieveFileOrFolderObject() through the uid-0 fallback storage, which the source marks for removal, and that is what the discouragement is about. So an EXT: path in f:image works and is tested, f:uri.resource is what a new template should use for a resource that needs no graphical operation, and a rule stated as "you must not use f:image for anything but FAL resources" is stronger than anything the code, the tests or the docblocks say.

hints.text: Cache busting belongs to the publisher rather than to the ViewHelper: SystemResourcePublisherInterface::generateUri() adds it while building the URI, from the file modification time for a package resource and from the sha1 for a FAL file. Every resource URI therefore carries one, a query string already written into the identifier no longer suppresses it, and useCacheBusting="false" on f:uri.resource is what switches it off.

An identifier is PKG:<composer name>:<path in the package>, EXT:<key>/<path>, FAL:<storage uid>:/<identifier>, an absolute URL, or URI:/<path> for one relative to the host. A bare relative path still resolves and is the predecessor form: below the public directory, or below the configured fileadmin and against the default storage only. A path inside an extension but outside Configuration, Resources/Private and Resources/Public is not addressable at all until Configuration/Resources.php declares it.

PublicResourceInterface is the public API of that world and is what a URI can be generated for. Core\Resource\File implements it beside the package types, so a FAL file and an extension file are handed to the same generation. Implementing it is not on offer — the interface reserves implementations for the core's own namespace, and a replacement is written as a SystemResourcePublisherInterface instead.

There is no resource object here: f:uri.resource takes a path and computes the URL itself through PathUtility, there is no f:resource ViewHelper to hand it one, and a URI carries cache busting only where the calling code put it there.
